sum: A restricted-area loop from Koto up a narrow gorge to the stone villages of Phu and Nar, then over the Kang La at 5,320 m to rejoin the Annapurna Circuit at Ngawal.

guide.note: Nar Phu is a restricted area. The permit is issued only through a registered trekking agency, and a licensed guide must accompany you throughout. Since March 2026 it can be issued to a single trekker, so you no longer need a second person in order to apply. Permits are checked at the police post in Koto. In practice the guide also arranges the few lodges, which often cannot be reached by phone, and makes the decision on the pass.

access: Most groups drive from Kathmandu to Besisahar and continue by jeep up the Marsyangdi road to Koto in one long day. The walk ends at Ngawal in the Manang valley, where a jeep can be arranged back down to Besisahar.

photo.a: Flat-roofed stone houses are stacked tightly up a rocky hillside above terraced fields, with a braided grey river beyond.
photo.c: Stone houses of a village in the Nar Phu valley

includes: porter in most packages (the cheapest tiers leave one out)
ACAP permit; the Nar Phu restricted-area permit in most packages (confirm)

permits.where: Department of Immigration in Kathmandu (the Pokhara immigration office also issues them), through a registered trekking agency only.

permits.name: Annapurna Conservation Area Permit
permits.where: Online at NTNC's e-permit site, or in person at the Tourist Service Centre in Bhrikutimandap, Kathmandu, and the Nepal Tourism Board office in Pokhara. A permit issued at a trail checkpost costs double.

transportText: Bus between Kathmandu and Besisahar both ways, and jeep seats up to Koto and back down from near Manang
tips: Bring a four-season sleeping bag. Lodge rooms in Phu and Nar are unheated and nights are well below freezing.
Carry microspikes and gaiters for the Kang La except in the driest weeks of October.
Take all the cash you will need from Kathmandu. There is no bank after Besisahar.
Ask before photographing people or the inside of monasteries, and leave a donation at Tashi Lhakhang and Nar Phedi.
Your agency needs your passport and visa a working day or two before departure to obtain the permit in Kathmandu.

days.note: A very long road day: six to seven hours to Besisahar, then five to six by jeep up the rough Marsyangdi road. The restricted-area permit is checked and registered at the police post in Koto. If you would rather not arrive at 2,600 m in one go, break the journey at Besisahar or Dharapani.

Cross the Marsyangdi and enter the Nar Khola gorge: pine forest, paths cut into the cliff, a stretch behind a waterfall, and lunch at the Dharmasala shelter. The last hour and a half climbs steeply onto the open shelf at Meta. The gain is almost 1,000 m, more than the usual rule allows, so go slowly.
why: Sleeping altitude rises 560 m, over the 500 m guideline, with no rest night before or after.

days.note: A long, rolling day past the winter settlements of Chyakhu and Kyang, with Annapurna II and Lamjung Himal behind you. Beyond Kyang the trail is cut into the cliff above the Phu Khola, then climbs past a tall rock pillar and through the old gateway to Phu. You are now sleeping above 4,000 m.

Stay two nights. Cross the river to Tashi Lhakhang monastery, walk the lanes of the village and, if you feel well, go an hour or two up the valley toward Himlung Base Camp before turning back. Going all the way to the base camp is a hard day of seven hours or more.

Retrace the trail down the Phu Khola past Kyang and Chyakhu, then turn off before Meta and drop to the Mahendra Pul, a bridge high above a narrow gorge. The monastery guesthouse is a little beyond it. Sleeping 600 m lower tonight gives your body a rest before Nar.

A short, steep morning. The trail zigzags up out of the gorge and passes rows of chortens before the fields below Nar. Arrive for lunch and spend the afternoon in the village. Tomorrow is the hardest day, so eat well, sort your gear and sleep early.

days.t: Over the Kang La to Ngawal
days.note: Leave by four. The path follows the valley west to the pastures at Kang La Phedi, then steepens over moraine and, often, snow to the pass, about 1,200 m above Nar. The far side drops very steeply on loose scree before easing onto grass. The descent to Ngawal is 1,660 m, so keep some strength for it.

Walk down to the road at Humde, under an hour, or have the jeep come up to Ngawal, then ride down the Marsyangdi through Pisang and Chame. With more time, walk on to Manang instead and continue round the Annapurna Circuit: you are already acclimatized for the Thorong La.

Six to seven hours by bus or private vehicle along the Marsyangdi and the Prithvi Highway. Traffic and roadworks on the highway can add an hour or two, so do not plan anything for the evening you arrive.
